entry.title: MOSA - Breaking Vendor Lock & Accelerating Innovation

link.title: MOSA - Breaking Vendor Lock & Accelerating Innovation

entry.content:
MOSA stands for “Modular Open Systems Approach.” It is an acquisition and technical strategy defined in a recent GAO report as “…a combination of engineering and business practices in which weapons systems are designed with modular components that are linked by clearly defined system interfaces.”

Although not a new concept (evidence shows DoD interest going as far back as 1994 with the Open Systems Joint Task Force) there is yet to even be a specific Wikipedia article for it! Despite the lack of Wiki-fame, it is required by law. As of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2017, programs are statutorily required to implement MOSA wherever practical.

Yet, a 2023 GAO report indicates implementation remains weak across the DoD portfolio. This post breaks down the two key features of MOSA, Modularity and Open Standard Interfaces, and how to identify the “MOSA Boundary” in real-world systems.

1. Modularity

To be modular means a system is defined by functional units that can be replaced with equivalent units as needed (e.g., during maintenance or upgrades).

The GAO provides a relatable analogy: The Kitchen. Appliances, such as a refrigerator, can be replaced or upgraded with a unit from any vendor. This is enabled because of:

  1. Standard Sizing: The fridge fits in the hole.

  2. Standard Interfaces: The 120V power outlet is universal.

MOSA seeks to apply these same benefits to the DoD weapons portfolio to break vendor lock and speed up technology insertion.

2. Open Standard Interfaces

The “Open Standards” requirement often raises the question: Where in the system must the interface be open?

The cleanest answer depends on your definition of the Line Replaceable Unit (LRU). As the name implies, an LRU is a component that can be replaced “on the line” (a term derived from the aerospace “flight line” where aircraft are parked/maintained).

  • Inside the LRU: Interconnections are of no concern to the integrator and can remain proprietary/closed.

  • Outside the LRU: Interfaces connecting the LRU to the platform must be Open.

Thus, defining the LRU enables discovery of the MOSA boundary.

Concrete Example: The Cockpit Display

Consider a basic display for an aircraft cockpit. It has two connectors on the back: Power and Video Input.

In this scenario:

  • The LRU: The entire display unit. If it breaks, the maintenance crew swaps the whole box.

  • The MOSA Boundary: The Power and Data connectors on the back panel.

  • Not MOSA: The ribbon cables inside the box connecting the LCD panel to the internal circuit boards.

A Systems Engineer can use System Boundary Diagrams to formally document which interfaces cross the LRU threshold and therefore require open standards.

Case Study: Proprietary Implementation of Open Standards

Imagine a scenario where an LRU uses a MIL-DTL-38999 compliant physical connector. The pins are assigned standard roles: DC power, RJ-45 Ethernet, and I2C. These are all openly published standards.

Is this connector MOSA compliant? The answer is: Maybe.

The complication is the Pin Mapping (the specific arrangement of signals). To determine compliance, we apply the Litmus Test:

The MOSA Litmus Test: If the government were to replace this LRU with one from a competitor—changing nothing else (like the cabling harness)—would it simply work?

  • Scenario A (Compliant): The original vendor provided the pin mapping with Government Purpose Rights (GPR) or Unlimited Rights. Competitors can see exactly which pin does what, allowing them to build a compatible drop-in replacement.

  • Scenario B (Non-Compliant): The physical connector is standard, but the specific pinout is proprietary to the original vendor. The government is now vendor-locked. Even though they use a “standard” connector, no one else can build a box that fits the existing cable harness without reverse engineering or paying royalties.

This is a critical edge case. On the surface, the hardware is “Open,” but the data rights regarding the implementation (the pinout) disqualify it. The priority solution is to comply with defined pinout standards (e.g., SOSA, GVA, VICTORY) or publish the Interface Control Document (ICD) with unlimited rights.

References

  1. GAO-25-106931: Weapon Systems Acquisition

  2. DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook (2025)
entry.summary: A quick overview of MOSA (Modular Open Systems Approach)

entry.title: Folk Theory and Horoscopes - A Review of Jungian Psychology Step by Step

link.title: Folk Theory and Horoscopes - A Review of Jungian Psychology Step by Step

entry.content:
The book Jungian Psychology Step by Step aims to introduce readers to Jung, but I found it poorly written…the literary equivalent of rambling. Much of the writing reminded me less of intellectual discourse and more of horoscopes.

Format aside, Jungian psychology itself felt to me more like folk theory, mysticism, and philosophy than actual science. Below are my thoughts on the introductory concepts that stood out.

The Collective Unconscious

The idea of a transcendent psychology from which common themes and archetypes are independently derived, the Collective Unconscious, is interesting, but ultimately strikes me as folk theory rather than an observable psychological phenomenon.

Archetypes

Stemming from the idea of the Collective Unconscious is the concept of “Archetypes.” These are common narrative characters Jung observed manifesting across cultures via their stories. Examples include the Hero (who undergoes the hero’s journey), the Wise Old Man/Woman (the “guide” character), and the Trickster (who causes chaos), amongst others.

The Shadow

The Shadow describes the aspects of our unconscious that we keep hidden, yet continue to follow us (like a shadow). Jung suggested “shadow work,” a process where individuals learn to recognize these dark traits on their journey toward “wholeness” or “individuation.” The goal is not to continue suppressing the shadow, but rather to recognize it and become conscious of it to improve one’s psychology.

Symbols and Myths

A recurring theme with Jung is the importance of symbols, myths, and religion. He argued that they represent the human psyche and studied them accordingly.

Synchronicity

Synchronicity is the concept of “meaningful coincidental encounters.” A famous anecdote from Jung himself involves a patient he described as being particularly rational. She was describing a dream where she was given a golden scarab; at that exact moment, a real, rare, scarab-like beetle flew into Jung’s office.

The event was so unlikely that it supposedly dissolved her rational barrier, allowing therapy to finally progress. Jung argued that such coincidences were connected by meaning rather than cause and effect. This idea is rightfully criticized as it implies metaphysical forces are at play. The the most charitable interpretation is that there are no metaphysics involved, but rather that coincidences become meaningful simply because they reveal something internal about us. Personally, I find this concept to be at high risk of confirmation bias.

Conclusion

Jungian Psychology seems to be a bridge between philosophy and the science of psychology, relying heavily on folk theory. While this makes his ideas less credible as hard science, they represent an interesting approach to understanding the mind, anchored deeply in the religious culture of his time.

entry.title: The Engineering of Learning - Immersion and Algorithms

link.title: The Engineering of Learning - Immersion and Algorithms

entry.content:
When I was in middle school, my obsession with anime led me to learn Japanese, as most shows were in Japanese with English subtitles. Because Japanese is often deemed one of the hardest languages for native English speakers to learn (and I wanted to understand it as fast as possible), I began researching the most effective methods for language acquisition. My research pointed to two major findings:

  1. Consistent Immersion (e.g., listening, speaking, and reading regularly).
  2. SRS (Spaced Repetition System) Flash Cards.

One surprise from this adventure was that it didn’t just teach me Japanese; it taught me how to learn across any domain. I have used these exact techniques to fast-track my preparation for the FE, CCNA, PE, and INCOSE SEP exams. Most recently, it allowed me to spin up at a new job quickly enough to lead a successful Critical Design Review (CDR) on a project I had only been involved with for a few months, enough so to win an award for excellence!

I want to share what I’ve learned about learning, and how these techniques can help you.

Immersion

The best way to learn Japanese is to live in Japan. Why? Because you are forced to read, speak, and hear the language every day. It takes discipline to recreate this immersion if you aren’t physically there, but today’s technology makes it easier than ever.

You can apply this same “digital immersion” to any domain. In my engineering career, this means exposure beyond the 9-to-5. I don’t just learn about RF systems at work; I read Wikipedia articles, watch YouTube deep-dives, and debate topics with AI models to test my understanding. The goal is to surround yourself with the topic constantly, creating a feedback loop that feeds into the SRS Flash Cards.

SRS Flash Cards

This is the “secret weapon.” SRS, or Spaced Repetition System, is an approach to flashcards that optimizes your memory. The algorithm forces you to review content you struggle with frequently, while pushing content you know well further into the future, ideally showing it to you right before you are about to forget it.

This planned repetition moves information from short-term to long-term memory efficiently. While many tools exist, the industry standard (and my personal favorite) is Anki.

The process is simple:

  1. The app shows you a card (which you create).
  2. You mentally guess the answer.
  3. You flip the card and rate how well you knew it (e.g., Did you forget entirely? Was it a struggle? Was it easy?).
  4. The algorithm schedules the next review based on your rating.

I do these flashcards every day, adding new cards whenever I encounter a new concept.

Example Workflow

Doing Flashcards

Every day, whenever I have free time whether its sitting on the couch, walking outside, standing in line, I pull out the Anki app on my phone. It can be mentally draining, so I often gamify it. For example, if I burn my “due cards” down to a certain number, I reward myself with 5 minutes of scrolling X (Twitter). I do this in bursts until all cards due for the day are finished.

Creating Flashcards

My deep study sessions involve reading articles or books and creating flashcards immediately when I hit a concept I need to retain—a new acronym, a definition, or a complex system interaction.

Recently, I have optimized this by using LLMs (like ChatGPT, Grok, or Gemini). I will discuss a topic with the AI, then ask it to generate copy-pasteable flashcards based on our conversation. I paste these directly into Anki. This helps solidify the questions and debates I’ve just had.

Why I use Anki

I stick with Anki for one main reason: Cloud Synchronization. I can review cards on my phone while out and about, sync to the server, and pick up exactly where I left off on my desktop. This seamless transition removes friction and enables the consistency required for the method to work.

Conclusion

This technique has drastically improved my life, not just for languages, but for mastering the technical requirements of my career quickly and permanently. The results speak for themselves, and I hope these techniques help you in your own continuous learning journey. Godspeed!

entry.title: A Systems View of History - Thoughts on ‘1493’ by Charles C. Mann

link.title: A Systems View of History - Thoughts on ‘1493’ by Charles C. Mann

entry.content:
Charles C. Mann’s 1493 is a dense look at the post-Columbian world. Rather than a full review, I want to capture the specific concepts that resonated with me, particularly regarding globalism as a complex system.

The Columbus expedition made our modern world

This topic was by far my biggest take away. Some interesting points follow:

  • The ‘world’ is a complex system outside of directed control. A fascinating example of emergence cited in the book is the ‘Little Ice Age.’ Mann suggests this may have been caused by the rapid decline of Native American populations due to European disease. This cessation of human-driven forest burning led to massive tree growth, carbon sequestration, and essentially cooled the planet.
  • The real “manifest destiny”, if there were such a thing, appears to be globalization. I originally believed it to be a recent phenomena made possible by technology such as large cargo ships, telephony, and the internet when in actuality it was already realized after Columbus connected the world through the Columbian exchange and simply amplified by modern technology. Regardless of trajectory, the endpoint was the globalization that we’re experiencing today.
  • Another emergent property of the globalization resulting from the Columbian exchange is the “Homogenocene”, the phenomenon where our world is becoming more “same” everywhere due to human driven globalization. Potatoes, tomatoes, and corn were once unique to the Americas but now are prevalent world wide and even form classical foods of many cultures outside the Americas.
  • Our modern world of spaghetti and red sauce Italian food, European potato cuisine, rubber plants being in South Asia was thanks to Columbus. Historical food staples of many cultures in Europe, China, and the Phillipines were really only “historical” as far back at post 1493!

On Slavery, Ethnicity, and Race

  • Race, as how it’s perceived in recent times and especially culturally, is a more modern phenomena. Mann argues that initially, the African slave trade was driven less by racial ideology and more by biological resistance to malaria and the ready supply of slaves resulting from the African slave trade. These circumstances made African labor an economically logical choice before it mutated into the chattel form of slavery that we know today. This resulted in some other interesting phenomena such as Africans being the majority people in the Americas for a period of time when most people going to Americas were the slave labor force for Tobacco and sugar plantations.
  • Indentured servants from Europe became disfavored for slaves because indentured servants often took land and became competition to the already established plantations after their contracts ended. They were also more prone to death due to the harsh conditions of the Americas.
  • Native American Indian slavery, already present in the new world, intensified due to their demand for flintlock guns from the West. The colonies needed labor and the tribes needed flintlock guns. This created a reinforcing feedback loop: tribes needed guns to survive, so they captured slaves to trade for guns, which required them to capture more slaves. This loop also resulted in competing colonies ally with competing tribes since the losing tribe would become slave labor for the “winning colony”, and likewise the winning tribe would then get flintlocks, further reinforcing this loop.
  • There was a complex relationship between black slave owners holding Native American Indians as slaves and Native American Indian slave owners holding black slaves beyond the traditionally well understood white slave owner dynamic.
  • In South America, escaped slaves resulted in new colonies resulting from mixing of African and the Native population, which would be called “Maroons”.
  • Also interesting was that slavery was not seen as morally abhorrent back then in the same sense it is viewed today and in fact there were even a whole different set of ethics applied to slavery (e.g. Christians could not enslave other Christians, Muslims could not enslave fellow Muslims, etc.)
  • People were typically more identified via their religion back then (e.g., Christians, Muslims) rather than the geography from where they came (e.g. Genoa, Spain)

The Galleon Trade

  • Trade was tough with China due to there simply being no demand for Western goods in China to begin with; they were satisfied with what they had until Western silver became available
  • China’s monetary instability (where new dynasties would render previous currency worthless) created an intense demand for silver as a stable store of value. The Americas had the supply, Spain controlled the logistics, and the Philippines served as the trade hub.
  • Eventually this made silver the mandatory currency for tax payments

Early American Colonial Life

  • That early life in the Americas was so dreadful due to mosquitos, malaria, swarms of ants, hostile native tribes, and difficulty in growing food. Large numbers of deaths were common.

Conclusion

Columbus changed the world more than just “discovering the Americas”. He essentially closed the last gap required to fully close the link to globalization, starting a series of world defining events such as the tobacco and sugar frenzy, slavery in the Americas, transportation of wildlife and plants between the continents, the resulting evolution of those plants (such as the tomato), the silver trade with China and economic impacts resulting thereof, and of course the rapid colonization of the Americas. The modern world is an emergent property of these complex, often brutal, historical exchanges. While we cannot change the suffering that fueled this globalization, 1493 provides a framework to understand how deeply connected our economic and ecological systems truly are. Capitalism continues to fuel modern globalism with supply and demand continuing to cut across borders.
entry.summary: My quick thoughts on 1493 by Charles C. Mann

entry.title: The Half-Way Handoff. A Simple Strategy for Seamless Team Cooperation

link.title: The Half-Way Handoff. A Simple Strategy for Seamless Team Cooperation

entry.content:
I wouldn’t claim to be a control freak, but if I could do everything myself, I would. I know I’m not alone in this sentiment; group project memes exist for a reason.

We know why this is. We know exactly what we want and how we want it. Relying on others often entails communication overhead, potential disputes, or simply being at the mercy of someone else’s schedule.

A great example that everyone in corporate America is familiar with is IT. It can be frustrating waiting for a ticket to be serviced when, if given the permissions, you could solve the issue yourself in five minutes by downloading a driver, installing a license, or just changing a setting.

Unfortunately, there is no way out of teamwork when working on complex engineering projects. It is simply impossible (and inefficient) to do all the work required for a major project by yourself. Reliance on the team is a necessity, so there needs to be a better way to manage it.

I want to share a solution that has worked well for me in overcoming the friction of getting team members to execute tasks. This method offers two key benefits:

  1. They are more likely to do the task.

  2. They are likely to do it sooner.

I call this technique the “Half-Way Principle.”

The Half-Way Principle

Preemptively completing a substantial portion of a request significantly increases the recipient’s willingness to finalize the task and accelerates the timeframe for its completion.

The “half-way” moniker is idiomatic; you don’t have to do exactly 50% of the work. You simply need to do enough to lower the activation energy for the recipient.

Examples in Action

Example 1: The Mechanical Housing You are an Electrical Engineer needing a housing designed by the mechanical team. Rather than just asking for “an enclosure,” you draw a rough concept in PowerPoint or document the specific physical requirements in text. You provide that to the mechanical team so they have something to immediately review, critique, or build upon.

Example 2: The Soldering Request You need a skilled technician to solder extremely small components onto a prototype board. When requesting their help, you don’t just hand them the board. You provide clear pictures of exactly what needs to be soldered and where, alongside a marked-up schematic they can use to validate the task.

This works because of physics: it takes more energy to start an object moving than to keep it moving. It is easier for a colleague to edit or correct a document than to stare at a blank page.

Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • It builds social capital. Team members appreciate the effort to make their lives easier, even if your initial draft was imperfect.

  • It breaks deadlocks. (I will elaborate on this in a future post).

  • Speed. Things get done sooner because you’ve removed the “I’ll get to it when I have time to figure it out” barrier.

  • Influence. You gain experience and influence by understanding the inputs required by other disciplines.

Cons:

  • More work for you. You are expending your energy to save theirs. However, you are trading effort for speed and certainty.

  • Capability requirements. You must have the basic tools and knowledge to start the task.

  • Lane variance. You must be careful not to step on toes or violate processes by operating outside your specific role.

Real World Case Study

I’ll end with a real scenario. I once needed an “ESI” (Engineering Special Instruction) from the Repair and Overhaul team while I was operating as a Systems Engineer.

I knew the R&O team would struggle to author the instructions because they didn’t know the new product or tools as well as I did. If I waited for them to learn it, the documentation would be delayed significantly.

Instead, I applied the Half-Way Principle. I wrote the the primary content myself. Since I was not in the Repair and Overhaul team, I could not “own” or release the document, but I provided all the inputs the R&O lead needed. All he had to do was copy the content into his organization’s templates and hit release.

I saved him from having to interview technicians, learn the tools, and interview me to elicit the information. In this scenario, I probably did most of the work, but the time savings for the project made it worth it.
entry.summary: A Simple Strategy for Seamless Team Cooperation
